data.title: Scabies — viva
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Scabies** (Infestations)_

**Q1. What is scabies? Describe the mite.**
- Intensely itchy contagious infestation by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis
- Female ~0.4 mm, burrows in stratum corneum, lays 2–3 eggs/day for 4–6 weeks; eggs hatch in 3–4 days; larva → nymph → adult in ~10–14 days
- Average 10–15 mites per patient in classic scabies; thousands to millions in crusted scabies; mites survive off host 24–36 h (longer in cool humid)

**Q2. How is it transmitted?**
- Prolonged skin-to-skin contact (family, sexual, care homes); fomites matter mainly for crusted scabies
- Incubation 3–6 weeks in first infestation; 1–3 days in re-infestation (already sensitised)

**Q3. Why does itching start late and get worse at night?**
- Itch is a delayed (type IV) hypersensitivity to mite, eggs and faeces (scybala) — takes weeks to develop
- Nocturnal itch: warmth of bed increases mite activity and itch perception

**Q4. Clinical features of classic scabies.**
- Generalised itching, worse at night, with other family members affected
- Burrows (pathognomonic): grey wavy thread-like lines 2–10 mm with a vesicle/dot at the end — web spaces of fingers, wrists, sides of fingers
- Papules, papulovesicles on finger webs, flexor wrists, elbows, anterior axillary folds, periumbilical, waist, buttocks, inner thighs, genitals (penile/scrotal nodules), areolae in women
- Circle of Hebra: imaginary circle through axillae, elbows, wrists, umbilicus, buttocks, genitals
- Head and neck spared in adults (involved in infants, elderly, immunosuppressed)

**Q5. Scabies in infants — how is it different?**
- Face, scalp, palms and soles involved; vesicles, pustules, nodules (axillae, groin); irritability, poor feeding; often misdiagnosed as eczema or infantile acropustulosis

**Q6. What is crusted (Norwegian) scabies?**
- Hyperinfestation in the immunosuppressed (HIV, HTLV-1, steroids, transplant), elderly, Down syndrome, leprosy, neurological disease with sensory loss
- Thick grey hyperkeratotic crusts and fissures on hands, feet, extensors, scalp, nails; little itch; highly contagious (millions of mites); can cause outbreaks in hospitals
- Treatment: oral ivermectin 200 µg/kg on days 1, 2, 8, 9, 15 (± 22, 29) + topical permethrin/benzyl benzoate with keratolytics; isolation and environment cleaning

**Q7. Name other variants.**
- Nodular scabies (persistent itchy nodules on genitals/axillae; hypersensitivity; may last months after cure — intralesional/topical steroid)
- Bullous scabies (mimics bullous pemphigoid in elderly), scabies incognito (steroid-modified), scabies of the clean (few lesions), animal scabies (Sarcoptes from dogs — no burrows, self-limiting)
- Secondary: impetiginisation (post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis — major problem in endemic communities), eczematisation, urticarial

**Q8. How do you confirm the diagnosis?**
- Clinical diagnosis using IACS 2020 criteria: confirmed (mite/eggs/faeces seen on microscopy or dermoscopy), clinical (burrows, male genital lesions, or typical lesions + itch + contact history), suspected
- Mineral oil scraping of a burrow → microscopy for mite, eggs, scybala
- Dermoscopy: 'delta-wing jet with contrail' sign (mite's head-legs triangle + burrow)
- Burrow ink test (ink fills the burrow)
- Skin biopsy rarely — mite in stratum corneum ('pigtail' of keratin), eosinophils

**Q9. Differential diagnosis.**
- Papular urticaria/insect bites, atopic dermatitis, prurigo, dermatitis herpetiformis, pediculosis, folliculitis, bullous pemphigoid (elderly), infantile acropustulosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis (infants), drug eruption, secondary syphilis (genital nodules)

**Q10. Treatment of classic scabies.**
- Permethrin 5% cream: apply from neck down (include scalp/face in infants and elderly) to entire body including under nails, web spaces, genitals; wash after 8–14 h; repeat after 7 days — first line, safe from 2 months of age and in pregnancy
- Oral ivermectin 200 µg/kg single dose, repeated after 7 days (two doses; not ovicidal) — not for <15 kg children or pregnancy/lactation
- Alternatives: benzyl benzoate 25% (dilute for children; 3 applications), crotamiton 10% (weak, antipruritic), sulphur 5–10% in petrolatum (infants, pregnancy; 3 consecutive nights), malathion 0.5%; lindane — avoid (neurotoxic)

**Q11. General measures for successful treatment.**
- Treat all household and close contacts at the same time, even without symptoms
- Wash clothes, bed linen and towels in hot water (≥50–60 °C) and dry in sun, or seal in a plastic bag for 72 h
- Cut nails; re-apply to hands if washed
- Antihistamines, emollients, mild steroids for post-scabetic itch; antibiotics for secondary infection

**Q12. What is post-scabetic itch and how do you differentiate it from treatment failure?**
- Itch can persist 2–4 weeks after successful treatment due to ongoing hypersensitivity to dead mite antigens — no new burrows, gradually decreasing
- Failure/reinfestation: new burrows or lesions after 2–4 weeks, contacts not treated, incorrect application, resistance — re-treat (consider ivermectin + permethrin)

**Q13. What is mass drug administration in scabies?**
- WHO strategy for endemic communities (prevalence >10%): ivermectin MDA (two doses 7 days apart) — reduces scabies and impetigo; scabies added to WHO NTD list in 2017

**Q14. Mechanism of action of permethrin and ivermectin.**
- Permethrin: synthetic pyrethroid — blocks sodium channels in mite nerve membranes → paralysis and death; poorly absorbed, low toxicity
- Ivermectin: binds glutamate-gated chloride channels in invertebrate nerve and muscle → hyperpolarisation, paralysis; does not cross human blood–brain barrier (P-glycoprotein); not ovicidal hence second dose

**Q15. Scabies in pregnancy and infants?**
- Permethrin 5% (safe), sulphur ointment; avoid ivermectin and lindane
- Infants under 2 months: sulphur 5% or crotamiton; apply to whole body including head

## Quick spotter facts
- Burrows in finger webs + nocturnal itch + family affected — scabies
- Delta-wing jet sign on dermoscopy
- Crusted scabies — millions of mites, little itch, highly contagious

## Note
Lindane withdrawal in India and ivermectin age/weight limits — please confirm with current guidance.

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Infestations — scabies); WHO / IACS guidance on scabies. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
